# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Repositioning leflunomide/teriflunomide (approved oral DHODH inhibitors for autoimmune disease) to overcome the differentiation blockade in primary AML via de novo pyrimidine-pool depletion

HYPOTHESIS: Leflunomide, via its active metabolite teriflunomide (A77 1726), reaches free plasma concentrations in humans that inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) in primary AML cells enough to deplete de novo pyrimidine synthesis, thereby inducing myeloid differentiation rather than nonspecific bulk killing.

BIOLOGICAL CONTEXT: Non-APL acute myeloid leukemia, tested as monotherapy on primary blasts (stratified by NPM1c, FLT3-ITD, TP53 status) with two distinct endpoints: (a) blast differentiation and (b) LSC-enriched/residual populations treated separately, because S2 shows cytarabine-resistant residual cells are metabolically, not hierarchically, defined and are not necessarily the ROS-low LSC state of S1 [S1, S2].

SUPPORTED PREMISES (from packet): (1) DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML models, establishing metabolism as a lever on the differentiation blockade [S4]. (2) Residual AML cells after chemo require oxidative metabolism; targeting that state changed response [S2]. (3) ROS-low quiescent LSCs show BCL-2-linked OXPHOS dependency [S1]; venetoclax-azacitidine is an established metabolism-targeting comparator, not part of this proposal [S3].

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (assumptions, each needing verification): (a) Approval facts recalled as unverified prior knowledge: leflunomide was approved for rheumatoid arthritis/psoriatic arthritis and teriflunomide for relapsing multiple sclerosis; both must be confirmed in FDA sources. (b) DHODH is an inner-mitochondrial de novo pyrimidine enzyme coupled to CoQ — textbook biochemistry, unverified in this packet. (c) Teriflunomide's heavily protein-bound free fraction overlaps its DHODH IC50 in AML cells — potency and free-drug numbers are unverified and are the central risk. (d) Pyrimidine depletion, not off-target effects, mediates differentiation. (e) Differentiation induction reduces clonogenic/LSC self-renewal rather than merely generating mature, drug-resistant cells.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS: Any observed effect could reflect bulk cytotoxicity; reported non-DHODH activity of A77 1726 on kinase signaling (unverified prior knowledge); generic mitochondrial/OXPHOS perturbation that mimics S1/S2 biology rather than pyrimidine starvation; or in vivo salvage from circulating nucleosides rescuing pyrimidine pools.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL TEST STRATEGY: Head-to-head comparison of teriflunomide, leflunomide, and brequinar (an unapproved benchmark DHODH inhibitor per packet logic [S4]) across ≥30 well-annotated primary AML specimens plus AML lines (e.g., MOLM-13, OCI-AML3) and healthy donor CD34+ progenitors. Mechanism readout: stable-isotope flux into UMP pools with uridine-nucleoside-rescue arms — on-target attribution requires that uridine abrogates both pyrimidine depletion and CD11b/CD14/CD15 induction. Function readouts: morphology, myeloid markers, apoptosis independence, CFU and long-term culture assays, and serial xenograft re-transplantation to test LSC burden. PK/PD in xenografts bridges achieved free concentrations to human steady-state exposure from the MS label (must be verified). A secondary exploratory arm tests additivity with azacitidine and with venetoclax-azacitidine as the reference metabolic regimen [S3]; repeating the approved combination itself is not the novel claim.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS (any one kills the hypothesis): (1) Teriflunomide/leflunomide at or below clinically estimated free concentrations fail to deplete UMP pools or induce CD11b in most specimens while brequinar succeeds — an exposure-limited failure of the drug–mechanism link. (2) Differentiation occurs but uridine does not rescue it — mechanism is not DHODH-mediated pyrimidine depletion. (3) Strong bulk differentiation without reduced serial xenograft re-initiation — the endpoint fails at the stem/residual-cell level anticipated by S1/S2.

SELECTIVITY AND TRANSLATIONAL LIMITATIONS: DHODH inhibition underlies the antirheumatic mechanism, implying toxicity risk in proliferating normal hematopoietic and lymphoid compartments — healthy CD34+ CFU and lymphocyte readouts are mandatory. Recalled, unverified label risks include hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity with prolonged washout due to enterohepatic recirculation, and the boxed teratogenicity warnings; pregnancy and hepatic exclusion criteria would apply. Protein binding makes free-fraction measurement, not total plasma concentration, the decisive exposure variable. LSC quiescence [S1] and the metabolic, non-stem identity of residual cells [S2] mean differentiation-driven responses may spare some residual disease, so monotherapy benefit is plausible mainly in bulk disease with additive benefit needing the combination arm.

VERIFIED VS PRIOR-KNOWLEDGE LEDGER: Verified here: only S1–S4 summaries. Everything about drug approval status, indications, potency, human exposure, label risks, and DHODH biochemistry is unverified prior knowledge requiring primary-source confirmation.

Final ranking:
1. Repositioning leflunomide/teriflunomide (approved oral DHODH inhibitors for autoimmune disease) to overcome the differentiation blockade in primary AML via de novo pyrimidine-pool depletion (promisingness 0.62, confidence 0.55; PMIDs: 27641501)

Repurposing bedaquiline, an approved antitubercular ATP-synthase inhibitor, to collapse oxidative phosphorylation in cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent residual AML

Hypothesis. Bedaquiline, approved for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (original indication; regulatory and pharmacology facts here are recalled prior knowledge, to verify), directly inhibits mammalian mitochondrial F1Fo-ATP synthase. In the post-cytarabine residual state described by Farge et al. — residual cells not enriched for leukemia stem cells (LSCs) but requiring oxidative metabolism with fatty-acid-oxidation-linked features [S2] — bedaquiline would deplete ATP at the terminal step of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and eliminate residual disease, with co-coverage of the ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent LSC fraction of Lagadinou et al. [S1] tracked as a separate endpoint. It is a direct-inhibition analogue of the venetoclax-azacitidine metabolic disruption reported as an established comparator [S3]; reusing that regimen is explicitly not the proposal.

Supported premises (packet evidence). (1) A functionally defined LSC subset is ROS-low, BCL-2-high and OXPHOS-dependent; reducing OXPHOS affects quiescent LSCs, an LSC metabolic vulnerability established only for BCL-2 inhibition, not for any other compound [S1]. (3) Metabolic disruption of LSC energy metabolism is clinically attainable, as shown for the comparator combination [S3]. (4) Metabolic inhibition can produce differentiation rather than killing, so myeloid differentiation markers are monitored as an alternative outcome channel [S4].

Explicitly speculative bridges. (a) Recalled prior knowledge needing verification: bedaquiline's antitubercular target is mycobacterial F-ATP synthase, and preclinical reports claim low-micromolar inhibition of human mitochondrial complex V; if unconfirmed, the mechanism premise fails. (b) Exposure bridge: free plasma concentrations at approved doses reach OXPHOS-suppressive levels (unverified; the drug is highly protein-bound and slowly cleared). (c) Dependency bridge: residual OXPHOS-dependent cells lack glycolytic reserve, so partial complex-V inhibition drops ATP below viability thresholds while more glycolytic cells compensate. (d) LSC bridge: because S1 places OXPHOS downstream of BCL-2, direct ATP-synthase inhibition might bypass the upstream BCL-2 node and co-target ROS-low quiescent LSCs — an extrapolation beyond the tested inhibitor class.

Alternative explanations. Any observed activity could instead reflect cationic-amphiphile off-targets (for example lysosomotropic stress), upstream electron-transport backlog with ROS rather than ATP depletion, nonspecific lipophilic cytotoxicity independent of metabolic dependency, or S4-like differentiation induction without net killing.

Discriminating preclinical test. In cytarabine-surviving residual populations from S2-type models, primary AML specimens stratified for ROS-low LSC content, normal CD34+ cells, and an OXPHOS-reliant versus glycolytic line panel, measure target engagement (oligomycin-sensitive respiration, cellular ATP, complex-V activity) against viability. Mechanism discrimination: galactose medium forcing OXPHOS reliance should sensitize cells to bedaquiline; ATP5A1/ATP5B knockdown should phenocopy the drug and occlude further drug effect; the structurally unrelated complex-V inhibitor oligomycin should show concordant metabolic and cytotoxic signatures. Context discrimination: bedaquiline administered after, not before, cytarabine should preferentially kill the residual oxidative-metabolism population, reduce LSC frequency in limiting-dilution assays, and be benchmarked against a venetoclax-azacitidine comparator culture [S3]. Window discrimination: paired normal CD34+ colony assays and cardiomyocyte or myotube ATP-suppression assays define the selectivity ratio; a patient-derived xenograft residual-disease experiment uses human-matched exposure and tracks residual burden, LSC frequency, CD11b/CD14 differentiation, cardiac safety, and whether ATP depletion precedes death.

Falsifying observations. The hypothesis is disconfirmed if: killing occurs without suppression of oligomycin-sensitive respiration or ATp-dependent respiration (off-target mechanism); galactose sensitization, genetic phenocopy, and oligomycin occlusion all fail (complex V not causal); cytotoxicity is equal in glycolysis-reliant bulk cells and normal CD34+ progenitors at free concentrations at or below clinically achievable levels (no dependency or no therapeutic window); or bulk residual disease shrinks while LSC frequency is unchanged (context claim falsified, consistent with the S2 caution). A single disconfirming result blocks the drug-mechanism-context link even if others pass.

Selectivity and translational limitations. S1 and S2 are model-dependent, and AML genotype heterogeneity is unaddressed. All bedaquiline-specific facts (MDR-TB approval, human complex-V potency, free-drug exposure, QT prolongation as dose-limiting toxicity) are unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation against regulatory and pharmacology sources before any clinical inference. Direct complex-V inhibition risks heart and muscle; high protein binding and a long half-life constrain exposure bridging and combination scheduling. Any existing preclinical AML reports of bedaquiline would change the novelty claim and must be checked. Established regimens remain standard of care; this hypothesis adds a mechanistic question, not a treatment recommendation.

Title: Conditionally repurposing bedaquiline, an approved antitubercular agent, to collapse oxidative phosphorylation in cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent residual AML — gated on verified human mitochondrial ATP-synthase inhibition and achievable free-drug exposure

Hypothesis (stated as a condition, not a premise). IF, at clinically achievable unbound concentrations, bedaquiline directly inhibits mammalian mitochondrial F1Fo-ATP synthase in AML cells, THEN it will deplete ATP at the terminal oxidative-phosphorylation (OXPHOS) step and preferentially eliminate the post-cytarabine residual, oxidative-metabolism-dependent disease state — cells not enriched for leukemia stem cells (LSCs), yet dependent on oxidative metabolism with fatty-acid-oxidation features [S2] — with co-coverage of the ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent LSC fraction [S1] tracked as a separate endpoint. Human complex-V inhibition is deliberately carried as a conditional test rather than a fact: it is unverified prior knowledge, verified first, before any AML work. Bedaquiline's original indication is multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, but every drug-level fact (approval, protein binding, half-life, QT prolongation, human complex-V potency) is unverified prior knowledge requiring regulatory and pharmacology confirmation. This is a direct-inhibition analogue of the venetoclax-azacitidine metabolic-disruption comparator [S3]; reproducing that regimen is not the proposal.

Supported premises (within packet limits). (1) An OXPHOS-linked, ROS-low, BCL-2-high LSC subset exists, and OXPHOS reduction affected quiescent LSCs; within the packet this dependency is demonstrated only for the tested BCL-2 inhibitor, and the BCL-2-OXPHOS relationship there is an association, not a proven causal ordering [S1]. (2) Cytarabine-resistant residual cells are not necessarily LSCs but require oxidative metabolism; altering that state changed response [S2], mandating separate bulk-versus-LSC endpoints. (3) Disrupting LSC energy metabolism is clinically attainable, as shown for the comparator combination [S3]. (4) Metabolic inhibition can promote differentiation rather than killing, so myeloid differentiation is monitored as an outcome channel [S4].

(a) Target bridge (assumption): recalled prior knowledge attributes bedaquiline's antitubercular effect to mycobacterial F-ATP synthase, and preclinical literature reportedly claims low-micromolar inhibition of human complex V; external input also suggests bedaquiline may already have been explored in oncology as a mammalian ATP-synthase agent. (b) Exposure bridge with a quantitative gate (assumption): regulatory PK at the approved dose (Cmax, free fraction; to be verified) will be converted to a projected unbound range, which must approach the measured intact-cell IC50 for oligomycin-sensitive respiration; margin will be allowed only for quantified intracellular/tissue accumulation, since extreme protein binding and slow clearance make this the weakest link. (d) LSC bridge: direct complex-V inhibition is an extrapolation beyond the only OXPHOS dependency supported in the packet (BCL-2 inhibition, an association); explicitly speculative.

Targeted search criteria: (bedaquiline OR TMC207) crossed with (acute myeloid leukemia; ATP synthase/cancer stem cells; residual disease). Gate 2, exposure: measured potency versus verified PK-derived unbound range for the approved dose; failure here falsifies the drug-level claim, not merely the context claim. This is a mechanistic hypothesis, not a treatment recommendation; established regimens remain standard of care.

1. Title: Repurposing teriflunomide (approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis) as a clinically achievable DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-starvation-driven myeloid differentiation in OXPHOS-high, cytarabine-residual AML and ROS-low leukemia stem cells, with respiratory flux reduction and BCL-2 dependence as separately falsifiable secondary hypotheses.

Hypothesis and biological context.
Teriflunomide — the active metabolite of leflunomide and, per unverified recollection requiring confirmation, an approved oral therapy for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (original indication; leflunomide itself is separately approved for rheumatoid arthritis, also unverified prior knowledge) — is proposed as a single-agent DHODH inhibitor for AML subsets defined experimentally by oxidative metabolism: ROS-low leukemia stem cell (LSC) fractions (S1) and cytarabine-surviving OXPHOS/fatty-acid-oxidation-high residual cells (S2). Primary mechanism, with class-level support from S4: clinically achievable teriflunomide exposures inhibit DHODH, drain de novo pyrimidine pools, and thereby force myeloid differentiation or loss of LSC function rather than nonspecific bulk killing. Importantly, the OXPHOS-high state is framed here as a susceptibility biomarker used to select patients and stratify response; the drug is not assumed to collapse respiration. Any respiratory effect is a distinct, testable secondary claim.

Supported premises (packet only).
S1: ROS-low LSCs are enriched for BCL-2 and OXPHOS dependency, and metabolic targeting can eliminate them in studied specimens. S2: cytarabine-resistant residual cells are OXPHOS/FAO-high, are not necessarily LSC-enriched, and metabolic-state alteration changed treatment response in those models. S4: DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML, with the caution that not every approved drug touching this pathway reproduces it. S3: venetoclax-azacitidine disrupts LSC TCA-cycle/OXPHOS metabolism and serves strictly as the established mechanistic benchmark; that regimen is not being proposed.

Explicitly speculative sub-hypotheses, each with its own discriminator.
(1) Respiratory-flux sub-claim: because DHODH transfers electrons to coenzyme Q (general biochemistry; verify independently), DHODH inhibition might secondarily lower mitochondrial oxygen consumption. Discriminators: an OCR drop should be reversed by uridine and attenuated when cells are rescued by an inhibitor-resistant DHODH allele and treated again. If OCR falls despite uridine and persists in resistant-DHODH-rescued cells, the sub-claim is falsified and any respiration phenotype is off-target ETC toxicity. (2) BCL-2-dependence sub-claim: S1 attributes LSC vulnerability partly to elevated BCL-2. BH3 profiling plus a venetoclax single-agent comparator arm will establish whether teriflunomide LSC activity is mechanistically separable from the BCL-2-axis vulnerability exploited by venetoclax-azacitidine (S3).

Exposure bridge as a gating step (the weakest premise).
Teriflunomide is reportedly highly protein-bound with a long half-life (unverified labeling recollection). Plan: (i) verify approved dosing and published free/total plasma concentrations; (ii) run the ex vivo screen in a broad provisional bracket (0.03–30 µM, 10-point doses) at 72 hours and 7 days, then tighten confirmatory testing to the verified clinically achievable free range; (iii) before any efficacy work, perform a reachability experiment in NSG mice dosed on the scaled approved schedule, measuring unbound plasma concentrations and intracellular dihydroorotate accumulation in xenografted blasts at steady state. In vivo efficacy and LSC-frequency arms proceed only if unbound levels meet or exceed the ex vivo active threshold; otherwise the proposal terminates on exposure grounds.

Prior-art verification and repositioned novelty.
Unverified prior knowledge requiring database checks: brequinar reportedly reached early clinical testing in AML decades ago, and leflunomide/teriflunomide may have preclinical hematology studies; if so, the differentiation axis is partially preempted. The contingent contribution is therefore: (a) the cytarabine-residual/LSC-frequency framing bridging S2 and S1 contexts, (b) salvage-capacity stratification, and (c) reconciliation of approved MS-dosing exposures with AML ex vivo potency and marrow reachability.

Quantified validation strategy.
1. Ex vivo screen across genotypes (FLT3-ITD, NPM1-mutant, TP53-mutant, MLL-rearranged): endpoints CD11b/CD14/CD64 induction, viability, S1-style CD34+CD38− ROS-low LSC gating, colony-forming assays. Pre-registered responder definition: at least 3-fold CD11b/CD14 induction (or at least 50% LSC-frequency reduction) with at least 60% viability retained and no full uridine reversal. Success rule: responders in at least 60% of evaluable specimens with a one-sided 95% binomial lower bound above 50%; fewer than 40% responders refutes clinical relevance of the ex vivo signal. 2. On-target engagement: LC-MS dihydroorotate accumulation and pyrimidine-pool depletion; Seahorse OCR with uridine-rescue, DHODH-knockout, and inhibitor-resistant-DHODH-rescue arms. 3. Salvage stratification: baseline ENT1/SLC29A1, SLC28 CNT, UCK1/2 and thymidine-kinase expression; exogenous uridine/nucleoside challenge in marrow-mimicking nucleoside conditions; correlate with response to address refractoriness by salvage. 4. Residual-disease assay: cytarabine pulse to generate S2-like survivors, then teriflunomide; test kill versus differentiation. 5. Comparator arms: brequinar (experimental reference), venetoclax single agent, venetoclax-azacitidine (S3 benchmark), cytarabine, vehicle. 6. Normal-cell window: normal CD34+ HSPC IC50 at least 3-fold above the AML geometric-mean IC50; toxicity in CD34+-engrafted mice. 7. In vivo: NSG xenografts with limiting-dilution LSC frequency, gated by the exposure step.

Alternative explanations and falsifying observations.
Alternatives: cytotoxic selection of already mature cells; reported non-DHODH activities at high concentrations (unverified); venetoclax-like primary ETC effects; salvage-mediated refractoriness. Pre-specified falsifiers: (a) no differentiation or LSC reduction at achievable exposures in most specimens; (b) all phenotypes fully uridine-rescuable, indicating pure antiproliferative cytotoxicity; (c) genetic DHODH manipulation neither recapitulates nor protects, indicating off-target mechanism; (d) OCR reduction is not uridine-rescuable or persists with resistant-DHODH rescue, falsifying the respiratory sub-claim; (e) normal HSPCs are more sensitive than blasts without a differentiation readout; (f) the exposure gate fails. Full prior-art preemption would weaken novelty rather than refute the mechanism.

Approval status, dosing, PK, and safety liabilities (teratogenicity, hepatotoxicity, immunosuppression — all unverified) require confirmation before translation; ex vivo differentiation may not predict marrow behavior; de novo pyrimidine dependence is heterogeneous; preclinical success cannot establish clinical efficacy or advantage over the established S3 regimen, and no established AML regimen is presented as a discovery.

Verified facts are the packet summaries [S1]-[S4]; all approval, pharmacokinetic, and prior-literature statements above are labeled unverified prior knowledge requiring direct checking.

Conditionally repurposing bedaquiline, an approved antitubercular agent, to collapse oxidative phosphorylation in cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent residual AML — gated on verified human mitochondrial ATP-synthase inhibition and achievable free-drug exposure

Hypothesis (stated as a condition, not a premise). IF, at clinically achievable intracellular unbound concentrations, bedaquiline directly inhibits mammalian mitochondrial F1Fo-ATP synthase in AML cells, THEN it will deplete ATP at the terminal oxidative-phosphorylation (OXPHOS) step and preferentially eliminate the post-cytarabine residual, oxidative-metabolism-dependent disease state — cells not enriched for leukemia stem cells (LSCs), yet dependent on oxidative metabolism with fatty-acid-oxidation features [S2] — with co-coverage of the ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent LSC fraction [S1] tracked as a separate endpoint. Human complex-V inhibition is deliberately carried as a conditional test, not a fact: it is unverified prior knowledge, verified first, before any AML work. Bedaquiline's original indication is multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, but every drug-level fact (approval, protein binding, half-life, QT prolongation, human complex-V potency) is unverified prior knowledge requiring regulatory and pharmacology confirmation. This is a direct-inhibition analogue of the venetoclax–azacitidine metabolic-disruption comparator [S3]; reproducing that regimen is not the proposal.

Primary novelty claim. The OXPHOS-collapse strategy is derivative of S1–S3 and oligomycin logic, and the drug-context pair alone is thin because bedaquiline has plausibly already been explored in oncology as a mammalian ATP-synthase agent (unverified prior knowledge; I cannot execute searches here). I therefore demote the drug-context pair from primary claim and elevate the sequenced residual-versus-LSC discriminating design, with pre-committed quantitative retention criteria: the hypothesis is retained only if bedaquiline given after cytarabine shrinks residual oxidative-metabolism disease by ≥50% versus vehicle and reduces LSC frequency by ≥5-fold in limiting-dilution assays, benchmarked against venetoclax–azacitidine comparator cultures [S3], all at exposure that suppresses normal CD34+ colony growth by ≤30%. Pre-committed search criteria remain (bedaquiline/TMC207 × AML; oncology/ATP synthase; residual disease); if prior oncology complex-V data surface, the claim reduces to this context-discrimination design and LSC co-coverage — a reduction the promisingness self-estimate below already anticipates.

Supported premises. (1) An OXPHOS-linked, ROS-low, BCL-2-high LSC subset exists and OXPHOS reduction affected quiescent LSCs; within the packet this dependency is shown only for the tested BCL-2 inhibitor, as an association, not a causal ordering [S1]. (2) Cytarabine-resistant residual cells are not necessarily LSCs but require oxidative metabolism; altering that state changed response [S2], mandating separate bulk-versus-LSC endpoints. (3) Disrupting LSC energy metabolism is clinically attainable [S3]. (4) Metabolic inhibition can induce differentiation rather than killing, so differentiation is a monitored outcome [S4].

Speculative bridges, each pre-committed to a test. (a) Target bridge: recalled mycobacterial F-ATP synthase attribution and low-micromolar mammalian complex-V potency are unverified; Gate 1 tests them. (b) Exposure bridge, the weakest link given extreme protein binding, now with a numeric decision rule fixed before AML work: Gate 2 passes only if verified unbound Cmax at the approved dose (ultrafiltration/equilibrium-dialysis PK) is ≥0.3× the intact-cell IC50 for oligomycin-sensitive respiration, OR if LC-MS/MS shows intracellular unbound-equivalent drug ≥1× that IC50 for ≥72 h at clinically relevant exposure in ≥2 primary AML specimens plus xenograft tissue; accumulation may override a failed plasma estimate only with this measured evidence. Selectivity gate, elevated from late discovery. Direct complex-V inhibition lacks venetoclax's BCL-2-dependency selectivity, so AML-versus-normal differential dependency is a gating premise: Gate 3 requires paired ex vivo respiration testing of diagnostic versus post-cytarabine specimens showing residual AML cells have ≥3-fold lower glycolytic reserve (oligomycin-induced ECAR rise) or ≥3-fold lower oligomycin IC50 than normal CD34+ progenitors before window testing proceeds.

Discriminating strategy (ordered gates; failure halts). Gate 1: purified human complex-V activity plus intact-cell oligomycin-sensitive-respiration IC50, before any AML work. Gate 2: exposure rule above. Gate 3: mechanism and dependency in cytarabine-surviving residuals [S2] and ROS-low-stratified primaries — galactose sensitization; ATP5A1/ATP5B knockdown phenocopy and occlusion; oligomycin concordance; methyl-pyruvate rescue of ATP and viability; LC-MS intracellular drug levels feeding the selectivity gate. Gate 4: context — bedaquiline after cytarabine shrinks residual disease, with ≥5-fold LSC-frequency reduction (limiting dilution), CD11b/CD14 induction [S4], and [S3] benchmark, applying the retention criteria. Gate 5: window — paired normal CD34+ colonies, cardiomyocyte/myotube ATP suppression, and a patient-derived xenograft residual-disease experiment at human-matched unbound exposure with serial ATP, residual burden, differentiation, plus hERG/ion-channel screening and ECG monitoring, because recalled QT risk is plausibly hERG-mediated and independent of ATP synthase (unverified prior knowledge). Lysosomotropic separation: matched cationic-lipophilic control compounds and lysosomal-pH readouts; killing tracking lysosomal alkalinization rather than ATP loss reclassifies the mechanism.

Falsifying observations. Cytotoxicity without suppression of oligomycin-sensitive respiration (off-target); combined failure of galactose sensitization, knockdown phenocopy/occlusion, and oligomycin concordance; methyl-pyruvate restoring ATP and viability in residual cells; intact-cell IC50 above the achievable intracellular unbound concentration; ≤3-fold differential dependency or killing between glycolytic bulk/normal CD34+ and residual AML cells (selectivity gate fails); residual-bulk shrinkage without ≥5-fold LSC reduction; or killing tracking lysosomal stress instead of ATP depletion.

Limitations. S1 and S2 are model-dependent; genotype heterogeneity is unaddressed; all bedaquiline-specific facts remain unverified prior knowledge. The numeric thresholds (0.3; 1×IC50/72 h; ≥3-fold; ≥50%; ≥5-fold; ≤30%) are pre-committed working assumptions chosen for decisiveness, not evidence. Direct complex-V inhibition plausibly threatens cardiac and skeletal muscle, and QT liability is assessed independently; tissue accumulation complicates scheduling. This is a mechanistic hypothesis, not a treatment recommendation; established regimens remain standard of care.

Final ranking:
1. Conditionally repurposing bedaquiline, an approved antitubercular agent, to collapse oxidative phosphorylation in cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent residual AML — gated on verified human mitochondrial ATP-synthase inhibition and achievable free-drug exposure (promisingness 0.45, confidence 0.50; PMIDs: 23333149, 28416471, 30420752, 27641501)

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide (approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; labeling and pharmacology unverified) as a DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-residual, OXPHOS-high AML with differentiation and LSC suppression as primary claims and OXPHOS reduction tested as a separable secondary sub-hypothesis.

CLAIM HIERARCHY AND CONTEXT. The OXPHOS-high state documented in S1 and S2 is treated strictly as a susceptibility biomarker, not as evidence that DHODH inhibition collapses respiration. Primary mechanistic claim: clinically achievable unbound teriflunomide exposures inhibit DHODH, deplete de novo pyrimidines, and produce (i) myeloid differentiation measurable at near-preserved viability and (ii) reduced LSC function in S1-style ROS-low CD34+CD38- fractions within cytarabine-residual AML. Secondary sub-hypothesis, explicitly speculative and independently falsifiable: because DHODH donates electrons to coenzyme Q (general biochemistry, outside the packet, unverified), on-target inhibition may reduce respiratory flux. The title asserts only the primary claim.

SUPPORTED PREMISES. S1: ROS-low LSCs are enriched for BCL-2 and OXPHOS dependency, and metabolic targeting can eliminate them in studied specimens. S2: cytarabine-resistant residual cells are OXPHOS/fatty-acid-oxidation-high but not necessarily LSC-enriched; altering that metabolic state changed treatment response. S4: DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML — the direct mechanistic foundation of the primary claim. S3: venetoclax-azacitidine disrupts LSC TCA-cycle/OXPHOS metabolism and is the established comparator; the plan deliberately keeps mechanisms separable from S3 (BH3 profiling, venetoclax single-agent arm, no combination) rather than conflating them.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (labeled). Bridge 1, load-bearing: approved dosing yields marrow-unbound teriflunomide at or above ex vivo target concentrations; recalled labeling suggests high protein binding and long half-life — unverified prior knowledge. Bridge 2: a differentiation component persists beyond the antiproliferative, uridine-rescuable effect; recalled from the brequinar literature, unverified. Bridge 3: cytarabine survivors remain de novo pyrimidine-dependent despite salvage; the packet does not address salvage, so this is assumption, not evidence.

PRIOR ART AND NOVELTY. The DHODH-differentiation axis is established by S4. Unverified prior knowledge suggests brequinar entered early-phase AML trials and that leflunomide/teriflunomide may have preclinical AML data. A mandatory targeted verification step (PubMed and registry searches: teriflunomide-AML, leflunomide-AML, brequinar-AML) precedes any novelty claim. If overlap exists, this proposal's contribution is repositioned as the S2 cytarabine-residual plus LSC-frequency framing, exposure-versus-IC50 reconciliation, and on-target genetic discrimination — none established in the packet.

QUANTIFIED PRECLINICAL STRATEGY. Step 0 (exposure gate): verify label, dosing, PK, and free fraction from public sources; pre-register concentration brackets spanning roughly 0.1x-30x the verified unbound plasma window at 6, 24, 72, and 168 h. Proceed only if blast IC50 for differentiation and viability falls at or below verified unbound exposure. In vivo gating: an NSG PK/PD cohort measures unbound plasma and intracellular dihydroorotate accumulation at approved dosing before any efficacy or LSC-dilution experiments are committed. Step 1: differentiation in at least 20 primary AML specimens across FLT3-ITD, NPM1-mutant, TP53-mutant, and KMT2A-rearranged strata versus normal CD34+ HSPCs; CD11b/CD14/CD64 with Annexin V. A specimen scores "differentiation" only if marker induction occurs with at least 90% viability retained (excluding cytotoxic selection of mature cells); pre-specified success rule: criterion met in at least 50% of specimens per genotype stratum; parallel S1-style CD34+CD38- ROS-low LSC gating. Step 2 (on-target triad): LC-MS dihydroorotate and pyrimidine pools; Seahorse OCR; uridine/nucleoside rescue; DHODH knockdown plus inhibitor-resistant DHODH allele rescue. Primary claim fails if all phenotypes are fully uridine-rescuable; the secondary OCR sub-hypothesis fails if the OCR drop is absent under resistant-allele rescue or fully rescuable by uridine, separating pharmacodynamic electron-flow coupling from downstream antiproliferative consequences. BH3 profiling places specimens on the S1 BCL-2-dependency axis, calibrated against venetoclax single agent. Step 3 (salvage stratification): baseline salvage signature (SLC29A1/2, UCK1/2, cytidine deaminase, DCK — unverified gene list) plus exogenous uridine challenge at measured marrow-mimicking nucleoside concentrations, used as a stratification variable in the primary analysis. Step 4 (residual disease): cytarabine pulse to generate S2-like survivors, then teriflunomide with and without uridine; record kill, differentiation, or neither. Step 5 (comparators): brequinar as on-target reference, venetoclax-azacitidine per S3, vehicle, cytarabine alone, venetoclax single agent. Step 6: NSG limiting-dilution xenografts for LSC frequency plus human CD34+ toxicity testing, run only after the in vivo exposure gate passes.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS. Primary claim fails if (a) the differentiation-plus-viability criterion is unmet in at least 50% of specimens at achievable exposures; (b) all phenotypes are fully uridine-rescuable; (c) DHODH genetic manipulation neither recapitulates nor rescues; (d) normal HSPCs are more sensitive than blasts without a differentiation readout; or (e) the exposure gate fails while brequinar shows the expected on-target profile. The secondary sub-hypothesis fails specifically on OCR rescue/genetic grounds, without necessarily invalidating the primary differentiation claim.

LIMITATIONS AND EVIDENCE STATUS. All approval, PK, half-life, and safety statements (teratogenicity, hepatotoxicity, immunosuppression) are unverified prior knowledge outside the packet. Ex vivo differentiation may not predict marrow behavior; de novo pyrimidine dependence is heterogeneous; positive preclinical data would not establish clinical efficacy or superiority over the S3 regimen. Verified here: only the packet summaries S1-S4; all other mechanisms, exposure claims, gene lists, and prior-art recollections require direct checking.

Final ranking:
1. Repurposing teriflunomide (approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; labeling and pharmacology unverified) as a DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-residual, OXPHOS-high AML with differentiation and LSC suppression as primary claims and OXPHOS reduction tested as a separable secondary sub-hypothesis (promisingness 0.58, confidence 0.62; PMIDs: 23333149, 28416471, 30420752, 27641501)

(b) DHODH is an inner-mitochondrial de novo pyrimidine enzyme coupled to CoQ — textbook biochemistry, unverified in this packet. (c) Teriflunomide's heavily protein-bound free fraction overlaps its DHODH IC50 in AML cells — potency and free-drug numbers are unverified and are the central risk. (d) Pyrimidine depletion, not off-target effects, mediates differentiation. (e) Differentiation induction reduces clonogenic/LSC self-renewal rather than merely generating mature, drug-resistant cells.

Mechanism readout: stable-isotope flux into UMP pools with uridine-nucleoside-rescue arms — on-target attribution requires that uridine abrogates both pyrimidine depletion and CD11b/CD14/CD15 induction. Repurposing bedaquiline, an approved antitubercular ATP-synthase inhibitor, to collapse oxidative phosphorylation in cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent residual AML

Hypothesis. Bedaquiline, approved for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (original indication; regulatory and pharmacology facts here are recalled prior knowledge, to verify), directly inhibits mammalian mitochondrial F1Fo-ATP synthase. In the post-cytarabine residual state described by Farge et al. — residual cells not enriched for leukemia stem cells (LSCs) but requiring oxidative metabolism with fatty-acid-oxidation-linked features [S2] — bedaquiline would deplete ATP at the terminal step of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and eliminate residual disease, with co-coverage of the ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent LSC fraction of Lagadinou et al. [S1] tracked as a separate endpoint. It is a direct-inhibition analogue of the venetoclax-azacitidine metabolic disruption reported as an established comparator [S3]; reusing that regimen is explicitly not the proposal.

Supported premises (packet evidence). (1) A functionally defined LSC subset is ROS-low, BCL-2-high and OXPHOS-dependent; reducing OXPHOS affects quiescent LSCs, an LSC metabolic vulnerability established only for BCL-2 inhibition, not for any other compound [S1]. (2) Cytarabine-resistant residual cells are not necessarily the LSC population but require oxidative metabolism; manipulating that state altered treatment response [S2], which anchors the disease context and forces bulk-versus-LSC endpoint separation. (3) Metabolic disruption of LSC energy metabolism is clinically attainable, as shown for the comparator combination [S3]. (4) Metabolic inhibition can produce differentiation rather than killing, so myeloid differentiation markers are monitored as an alternative outcome channel [S4].

Explicitly speculative bridges. (a) Recalled prior knowledge needing verification: bedaquiline's antitubercular target is mycobacterial F-ATP synthase, and preclinical reports claim low-micromolar inhibition of human mitochondrial complex V; if unconfirmed, the mechanism premise fails. (b) Exposure bridge: free plasma concentrations at approved doses reach OXPHOS-suppressive levels (unverified; the drug is highly protein-bound and slowly cleared). (c) Dependency bridge: residual OXPHOS-dependent cells lack glycolytic reserve, so partial complex-V inhibition drops ATP below viability thresholds while more glycolytic cells compensate. (d) LSC bridge: because S1 places OXPHOS downstream of BCL-2, direct ATP-synthase inhibition might bypass the upstream BCL-2 node and co-target ROS-low quiescent LSCs — an extrapolation beyond the tested inhibitor class.

Alternative explanations. Any observed activity could instead reflect cationic-amphiphile off-targets (for example lysosomotropic stress), upstream electron-transport backlog with ROS rather than ATP depletion, nonspecific lipophilic cytotoxicity independent of metabolic dependency, or S4-like differentiation induction without net killing.

Discriminating preclinical test. In cytarabine-surviving residual populations from S2-type models, primary AML specimens stratified for ROS-low LSC content, normal CD34+ cells, and an OXPHOS-reliant versus glycolytic line panel, measure target engagement (oligomycin-sensitive respiration, cellular ATP, complex-V activity) against viability. Mechanism discrimination: galactose medium forcing OXPHOS reliance should sensitize cells to bedaquiline; ATP5A1/ATP5B knockdown should phenocopy the drug and occlude further drug effect; the structurally unrelated complex-V inhibitor oligomycin should show concordant metabolic and cytotoxic signatures. Context discrimination: bedaquiline administered after, not before, cytarabine should preferentially kill the residual oxidative-metabolism population, reduce LSC frequency in limiting-dilution assays, and be benchmarked against a venetoclax-azacitidine comparator culture [S3]. Window discrimination: paired normal CD34+ colony assays and cardiomyocyte or myotube ATP-suppression assays define the selectivity ratio; a patient-derived xenograft residual-disease experiment uses human-matched exposure and tracks residual burden, LSC frequency, CD11b/CD14 differentiation, cardiac safety, and whether ATP depletion precedes death.

Falsifying observations. The hypothesis is disconfirmed if: killing occurs without suppression of oligomycin-sensitive respiration or ATp-dependent respiration (off-target mechanism); galactose sensitization, genetic phenocopy, and oligomycin occlusion all fail (complex V not causal); cytotoxicity is equal in glycolysis-reliant bulk cells and normal CD34+ progenitors at free concentrations at or below clinically achievable levels (no dependency or no therapeutic window); or bulk residual disease shrinks while LSC frequency is unchanged (context claim falsified, consistent with the S2 caution). A single disconfirming result blocks the drug-mechanism-context link even if others pass.

Selectivity and translational limitations. S1 and S2 are model-dependent, and AML genotype heterogeneity is unaddressed. All bedaquiline-specific facts (MDR-TB approval, human complex-V potency, free-drug exposure, QT prolongation as dose-limiting toxicity) are unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation against regulatory and pharmacology sources before any clinical inference. Direct complex-V inhibition risks heart and muscle; high protein binding and a long half-life constrain exposure bridging and combination scheduling. Any existing preclinical AML reports of bedaquiline would change the novelty claim and must be checked. Established regimens remain standard of care; this hypothesis adds a mechanistic question, not a treatment recommendation.
